title: Home to his mother
hookLine: the baby refuses every nurse until his sister leads them to his own mother
last: A GOOD HEART IN A HARD HOUSE.

cards: Back upstream, in a small house, a mother sits very still. She's set her son on the river, and the Qur'an is plain about what that costs: the heart of Musa's mother became empty. Hollowed out.
So empty she nearly gave the whole secret away, and would have, the verse says, if Allah hadn't strengthened her heart. But she doesn't just sit.
She turns to her daughter, Musa's sister, and gives her one word: follow him.

teach.b: Surah al-Qasas keeps going. The sister watches from a distance, the Qur'an says, while they didn't notice her. Picture a girl at the edge of a crowd at the palace, trying to look like she's just passing by.
Inside, there's a problem. The baby won't nurse.
Nurse after nurse is brought in, and he turns away from every one. The Qur'an says Allah had forbidden him the foster mothers beforehand. So the sister sees her chance.

teach.h: SHALL I SHOW YOU A HOUSEHOLD?
teach.b: She steps forward, as innocently as she can: shall I show you a household who will raise him for you and take good care of him?
And so, the verse says, We returned him to his mother, so that her eye might be cooled, and she would not grieve, and so she would know that the promise of Allah is true.
On day forty-three, at the river, she was promised: We will bring him back to you. Here it is, a few verses later.
And yesterday's image is back too: her eye cooled, the same delight Asiya felt, now given to the woman who bore him. Notice who makes it happen. Not an army, not a miracle anyone can see.
A baby who won't feed, and a sister brave enough to speak up at the right moment. The Qur'an doesn't give the sister's name, and says no more about her after this. But without her, no homecoming.
Some commentators add that the mother was even paid to nurse her own son. The text itself only says he came home.

how: Muslims often point to Musa's return to his mother as a sign that Allah's promises are kept, and teachers use the story with children to talk about trust.

o: a baby his sister carried back home across the Nile
a baby the palace sent off to a desert tribe
the baby who refused every nurse until he came home

games.q: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.
p: We will bring him back to you

s: she is unnamed, and the Qur'an says no more about her after this.
the Qur'an admits his mother nearly gave the secret away
her heart became empty, and she nearly revealed it, until Allah strengthened her heart.
the palace found his mother by searching the city
his sister stepped forward and offered a household who would raise him.

games.q: you're Musa's sister, watching from the edge of the crowd. the baby won't nurse from anyone they bring. what do you do?
o: run home and tell your mother to hide.
step forward and offer a household who will care for him.
keep watching. it isn't safe to speak.
games.why: she said: shall I show you a household who will raise him and take good care of him? and so he came home to his mother, just as she'd been promised.

practice: Think back for something you lost, let go of or gave up on that found its way back: a friendship that restarted after years, a thing misplaced for a month, a sense of humor after a bad season, your appetite for something you used to love.
Notice who or what carried it home; often it's someone small, standing at the edge of the crowd. If you pray, give thanks for it.

wordCard.voice: Musa, the baby who refused every nurse until his sister brought him home, his mother's eye cooled at last.

orig.note: Arabic, from Qur'an 28:10: "empty" — the heart of Musa's mother after she let him go.

carryVoice: Your line: what is yours returns. A heart emptied out, and a promise kept. Day forty-five, done.
